title: A pricing page for a small consultancy
metaTitle: A small consultancy pricing page that shows fit
excerpt: Show what the fee includes, what the buyer still does, and how to book a working session. They are judging fit against doing it themselves, not doing arithmetic.
alt: A hand holding a blue pen over wireframe sketches, with a mug and a closed notebook nearby, a working page rather than a hidden quote.
caption: The fee should be as plain as notes on the table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Should a small consultancy publish fees?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape even when the final amount depends on the problem. Say whether the work is a fixed session, a bounded project, or a retainer, what the buyer stops doing, and what they still own. A page that only says custom does not let them compare you with doing it themselves.

faqs.question: What belongs in included and not included?
faqs.answer: Inclusions should name the work they would otherwise do, such as a decision written in their words and notes their team can reuse. Exclusions should use the same size type and cover real leftovers, such as rollout or a second problem. Only list an edge you will enforce.

faqs.question: What should the pricing page ask them to do next?
faqs.answer: Ask them to book the working session, not to request a quote you have already described. The next screen should restate the length, the outcome, and the fee shape. Do not send them to a scheduler whose title is a generic intro unless that is truly the offer.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A small consultancy pricing page is where a buyer comparing you with doing the work themselves judges fit. They are not there to do arithmetic. They want to know what the fee includes, what it leaves on their desk, and how to book a working session. If the page says only "custom," they assume the number will appear after they have already spent the hour they were trying to save. Google's helpful-content guidance asks whether a page is a substantial description of the topic, and whether the reader leaves able to take the next step. A fee page that hides the shape fails both.

Say the shape in the first screen. A fixed session. A project with an end. A retainer with a boundary. What is inside. What they still do. Then one action: book the working session. The rest of the page can explain the edges. It should not be required reading before the shape is visible.

## The comparison is their time

This buyer already has a price in mind, and it is not your rate card. It is their Tuesday. They are asking whether hiring you is safer and faster than another month of doing the problem themselves, badly, between other jobs. A table of tiers named Bronze and Gold does not answer that. A plain account of what they stop doing does.

Write the opening as three lines they can repeat to a co-founder.

- The shape: a fixed session, a bounded project, or a retainer.
- What they no longer have to do themselves if they pay it.
- What they still own after you leave the room.

You do not have to print a single number if every engagement truly differs. You do have to print the shape. "We tailor our fees" is not a shape. "The working session is a fixed fee. A project, if you want one, is scoped after that session and has an end date" is a shape. If you publish a number, define what it buys. Hours are not a result. A decision they can send is a result.

Leave the calculator off. A slider that multiplies days by a rate trains them to haggle the rate instead of judging the problem. If you sell days, say how a day is used and what a day does not include. If you do not sell days, do not dress the page as a day-rate menu because other firms do.

## Included means the work they would have done

"Strategic support" is not an inclusion. Name the work they would otherwise do on a Sunday.

A diagnosis of the stuck decision, written in their words. A session with the person who can say yes, not a survey of the staff. A recommendation they can accept or reject in the room. The notes, in a form their team can reuse. One named person from your side who stays through that decision.

Put the inclusions in the order the work happens. Do not sort them by how impressive they sound. "Proprietary frameworks" is an internal boast. "You leave with the price list you were avoiding, written so a salesperson can send it" is an inclusion they can check against doing it themselves.

If some work includes implementation and some stops at the decision, say which fee includes which. A buyer who might DIY treats a blurred bundle as a later invoice, or as a trap that never ends. Two short columns are enough: we do this, you still do this. A paragraph that mixes both will be misread. They are hunting for the line that means the project never finishes.

## What is not included, in the same size type

The exclusions are how this buyer trusts you. They are afraid of a retainer that becomes a job they cannot cancel, and of a deck they still have to turn into a decision. Write the edges in the same size type as the inclusions. A footnote is where the surprise lived last time.

Common edges, if they are true:

- Rollout, training, or the weekly meeting after the decision.
- Work outside the named problem, including the adjacent mess they mention in passing.
- Their staff's time, which you cannot spend for them.
- A second problem discovered in the room, unless you scope it after.
- Tools, ads, or vendors you might recommend.

Only list an exclusion you will enforce. A page of theoretical exclusions looks like a contract dumped on the web. Pick the ones a DIY buyer uses as reasons to stay in-house. "You will still have to run the Monday meeting" is an honest exclusion. It also shows you are not pretending to become their operator.

Say what happens if they stop. If a session fee is earned when the session happens, say that. If a project can be paused at a milestone, say which milestone and what they keep. Ambiguity here is how a small engagement becomes a dispute. The page is not the agreement. It can stop the first conversation from being a trap.

## Do not hide a shape they will ask for

Some principals worry a visible fee scares off good clients. The client who leaves because the shape is wrong was going to leave after you had prepared a proposal. The client who stays will book a session that matches the problem. That is the fit the page is for.

There is a real limit. Do not publish a number the team will not honor. Do not publish a band so wide it says nothing. A band is useful when it maps to the problem you named on the homepage. If you cannot defend the band, describe the shape and invite the session.

Google's title-link guidance says each page needs descriptive title text, and that vague labels do not help anyone choose a result. "Pricing" is a vague label, in the same family as "Home." "What a working session costs" or "How a project is billed" tells the buyer they are in the right place. Google may build the title link from the title element, the visible heading, or other prominent text when those disagree. Make the heading and the title element say the same thing. Do not stuff the title with every industry you have touched. Repeated keywords make the result look spammy, which the same guidance warns against.

One large heading. Then the shape. Then what they stop doing. If "Our philosophy" and "Fees" are the same visual size, a stranger cannot tell which is the page.

## The session is the next step, not a quote button

The action is to book the working session. "Request a quote" suggests the price is a prize withheld until a form is filled. You have already shown the shape. The session is how you learn whether this problem matches it.

The button can say "Book a working session." The next screen should say how long it is, what they leave with, and what to bring: the decision they have postponed, and who else must say yes. Repeat the fee shape in one sentence so the booking is not bait. If a problem is billed differently, say so and point to the offer, once.

Do not add a PDF fee schedule that disagrees with the page. If finance needs a document, generate it from the same sentences. A chat widget that opens with "How can we help?" throws away the shape. If you use a scheduler, the event title should be the session, not "intro call," unless an intro is truly what they get.

## Packages that pretend to be a menu

Three packages are a menu. A menu invites comparison shopping among your own tiers, which is arithmetic, not fit. Use packages only when a buyer can tell which problem each one solves, and when the boundary between them is a real difference in the work, not a difference in the number of workshops.

If you have one problem and one shape, publish one shape. A single clear offer is easier to compare with doing it themselves than a grid. The grid looks like choice and feels like a brochure. The buyer who is protective of their calendar will not study it. They will leave, or they will book the cheapest tier and expect the expensive outcome.

Name the condition under which the shape changes. A session is fixed. A project exists only after the session, with an end. A retainer exists only when the decision has to be revisited monthly, and it has a review date. Those are conditions. They are not three logos.

## Check the page against the last invoice

Put the last three invoices next to the draft. Every line on an invoice should be predictable from the page. If the invoice has a line the page never mentions, add it to inclusions or exclusions, or stop charging it.

Read the page to someone who has done this kind of work themselves and has not hired you. Ask what they would pay, when, what would surprise them, and what they would do next. If they cannot answer the first two, the shape is buried. If they say they would email for a quote, the action is still a hallway.

Fix the opening. Do not add a sixth paragraph of reassurance under a weak first screen. A fee page that begins with your philosophy will be judged before the shape appears. Put the shape first.

The fee still needs offers with edges. Read [how each offer should state what the buyer stops doing](/blog/the-services-page-a-small-consultancy-actually-needs) before you publish a shape with no named problem under it.

If you want a second pair of eyes on how a fee page is structured, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the shape you are willing to say in public.
